content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to self-evaluate retrieval quality by capturing uncertainty. Almost all previous works use similarity as the only criterion to conduct image-text retrieval or matching. Naturally, the pair with the highest pair-wise similarity is considered as correct retrieval, even if the retrieval is wrong or unreliable. This is actually difficult to decide correctly. Motivated by this, the authors endow the model with this capability by utilizing evidence deep learning (EDL) to quantify uncertainty for cross-modal retrieval. Meanwhile, extensive experiments are conducted on two widely used cross-modal datasets (Flickr30K and MS-COCO) to verify the superiority and effectiveness of the proposed method. Moreover, some qualitative results (e.g., the relatively high similarity with high uncertainty) are given in the experiments, which could provide some insightful evaluation.  Overall, this work is interesting and novel.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. By utilizing evidential deep learning to quantify uncertainty in image-text matching, the motivation for trustworthy retrieval is interesting and applicable. The method introduces a new perspective (point) for evaluating retrieval quality, i.e., uncertainty, not only similarity, which provides self-evaluation for cross-modal learning.
2. The authors solve some challenges of utilizing evidential deep learning from classification tasks to cross-modal retrieval, e.g., the difference between instance-level and category-level evidence quantification, and the optimization challenge of bi-directionality when applying EDL in VSE.
3. Moreover, the experiments are detailed and reasonable, especially some retrieved cases with high and low uncertainty are given for self-evaluation.

Weaknesses:
1. This paper lacks a summary of related works. Although the authors review some works in the INTRODUCTION (e.g., VSE-based methods, the methods using complex similarity inference, etc.), it is still not sufficient to comprehensively review the existing works.
2. The authors use a data augmentation strategy for image-text representation learning, but there is a lack of further discussions, such as the augmentation rate (AR.) mentioned in the paper.
3. This work conducts Max Pooling to aggregate features for visual semantic embedding. The recent work (i.e., VSE$\infty$) proposed a Generalized Pooling Operator (GPO) to aggregate image and text features and achieve good performance. Could GPO or other pooling strategies replace Max pooling to achieve higher performance?

However, the actual instance number is much larger than the batch size. Thus, when considering a much larger number of negative pairs in full instance-level retrieval, the big negatives may bring more uncertain information leading to negative effects. content.comment:
**Q4: As shown in Fig.6-b, the more times the consistency module is performed, the better the performance. Why didn't the authors choose more “MaxTimes” in the experiments?**

**R4:**  In our method, every additional consistency module requires one more feature embedding used for the generation of opinions, thus leading to extra time costs. That is to say, if the "MaxTimes" is too large, the training time cost would be very high. From Fig.6-b, one could find that when $MaxTimes$ is set to 3∼6, the performance gap is not large, which indicates that extra time cost could not bring considerable improvement. To tradeoff the time cost and performance, we set $MaxTimes$ to 3 in our experiments.

**Q5: In the paper, the authors employ K-way classification in mini-batches with a fixed size to simulate instance-level retrieval. However, the actual instance number is much larger than the batch size. Thus, when considering a much larger number of negative pairs in full instance-level retrieval, the big negatives may bring more uncertain information leading to negative effects. How does this work tackle this gap between simulated classification and real retrieval?**

**R5:** Thanks for your insightful comments. Inspired by contrastive learning, we regard the cross-modal retrieval as a $K$-way classification in a mini-batch. That is to say, a query (probe) from a modality is classified by a gallery (retrieval) set from another modality, where each instance pair is treated as the same class. To simulate classification, the negative class is actually equivalent to the negative pair. During the training, we can naturally achieve the goal of image-text matching by performing probabilistic optimization, i.e., maximize positive pair similarity and minimize negative pair similarity. In the inference stage, we can utilize the similarity to complete the retrieval. However, In standard classification scenarios, empirically, the performance tends to drop as the number of negative classes increases, however, in image-text matching, more negatives could provide more reliable hard negative pairs to improve performance. To investigate the impact of batch size, we conduct the comparison experiments as shown in the following table. From the results, one could find that the performance of our method does not improve with increasing batch size.

|            | I2T   | I2T   | I2T   | T2I   | T2I   | T2I   |        |
|------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|--------|
| Batch size | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | rSum   |
| 32      | 77.0  | 94.8  | 97.7  | 57.1  | 83.7  | 90.5  | 500.8  |
| 64      | 79.4  | 95.4  | 97.3  | 58.8  | 84.9  | 90.5  | 506.3  |
| 128     | 80.3  | 95.5  | 97.8  | 59.7  | 85.1  | 90.9  | 509.3  |
| 256      | 81.1  | 95.9  | 98.3  | 59.8  | 85.0  | 90.8  | 510.9  |
| 384      | 79.1  | 95.0  | 97.8  | 58.4  | 83.8  | 90.5  | 504.6  |
| 512     | 79.7  | 94.1  | 97.4  | 57.4  | 83.1  | 90.1  | 501.8  |

To ensure fairness, we follow the same batch size as the previous methods [1-4] in our all experiments, i.e., $K=128$.

**References:**

>[2] Faghri, Fartash, et al. "Vse++: Improving visual-semantic embeddings with hard negatives." arXiv preprint arXiv:1707.05612 (2017).\
>[3] Lee, Kuang-Huei, et al. "Stacked cross attention for image-text matching." Proceedings of the European conference on computer vision (ECCV). 2018.\
>[4] Diao, Haiwen, et al. "Similarity reasoning and filtration for image-text matching." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 35. No. 2. 2021.

Thank you for your recognition of our work and valuable comments. Attached is our point-by-point response.

**Q1: This paper lacks a summary of related works. Although the authors review some works in the INTRODUCTION (e.g., VSE-based methods, the methods using complex similarity inference, etc.), it is still not sufficient to comprehensively review the existing works.**

**R1:** Thanks for your insightful suggestion, we will provide a discussion about the related works in the appendix. Most of the existing popular methods for image-text matching (ITM) could be roughly divided into two groups, i.e., the global-level methods represented by visual-semantic embeddings (VSE) and the local-level methods with complex similarity inference. The global-level methods mainly aim to obtain good representations from visual and textual modalities,  e.g., VSE$\infty$ [1] and VSE++ [2]. The local-level methods mainly learn the latent fine-grained alignments across different modalities for more accurate similarity inference, e.g., SCAN[3] and SGRAF[4].

**Q2: The authors use a data augmentation strategy for image-text representation learning, but there is a lack of further discussions, such as the augmentation rate (AR.) mentioned in the paper.**


**R2:** Following VSE$\infty$[1], we conducted the same data augmentation strategy (i.e., "Discard", "Mask", and "Swap") in our experiments. To be specific, for images, some extracted region proposals are randomly discarded according to a given probability, i.e., the augmentation rate (AR). For sentences, some words are randomly discarded, masked, or swapped with each other. The data augmentation is only utilized during the training stage, but not during testing. In order to investigate the impacts of data augmentation versus different ARs, we conduct the parameter analysis experiments as follows:
|     | I2T   | I2T   | I2T   | T2I   | T2I   | T2I   |        |
|-----|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|--------|
| AR. | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | rSum   |
| 0.1 | 79.6  | 95.4  | 97.8  | 58.7  | 84.4  | 90.4  | 506.3  |
| 0.2 | 80.3  | 95.5  | 97.8  | 59.7  | 85.1  | 90.9  | 509.3  |
| 0.3 | 79.2  | 94.9  | 97.8  | 59.7  | 85.2  | 90.8  | 507.6  |
| 0.4 | 78.8  | 94.2  | 97.2  | 59.1  | 84.6  | 90.4  | 504.3  |
| 0.5 | 77.6  | 93.5  | 96.7  | 57.1  | 83.2  | 89.7  | 497.8  |

From the table, one could draw that the data augmentation should be in a suitable range, otherwise too strong or too weak will drop the performance.

**Q3: This work conducts Max Pooling to aggregate features for visual semantic embedding. The recent work (i.e., VSE) proposed a Generalized Pooling Operator (GPO) to aggregate image and text features and achieve good performance. Could GPO or other pooling strategies replace Max pooling to achieve higher performance?**

**R3:** Thanks for your valuable comment. To further study the impacts of different aggregation strategies, we replaced $Max Pooling$ of our TcVSE with $GPO$ [1], $AvgPooling$, and $K-MaxPooling (K=10)$ for experiments. The results are as follows:

|                       | I2T   | I2T   | I2T   | T2I   | T2I   | T2I   |        |
|-----------------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|--------|
|                       | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | rSum   |
| TcVSE w/ AvgPooling   | 67.2  | 89.2  | 94.2  | 47.9  | 77.0  | 85.5  | 461.0  |
| TcVSE w/ K-MaxPooling | 73.8  | 92.4  | 96.1  | 52.7  | 80.0  | 87.4  | 482.4  |
| TcVSE w/ GPO          | 80.7  | 95.1  | 97.9  | 59.3  | 84.9  | 91.1  | 509.0  |       
| TcVSE                 | 80.3  | 95.5  | 97.8  | 59.7  | 85.1  | 90.9  | 509.3  |

From the table, our TcVSE did not gain a significant improvement from GPO, and even with a slight performance drop. Thus, we choose $Max Pooling$ with lower computational cost as the aggregate strategy in TcVSE.


**References:**
>[1] Chen, Jiacheng, et al. "Learning the best pooling strategy for visual semantic embedding." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2021.\
>[2] Faghri, Fartash, et al. "Vse++: Improving visual-semantic embeddings with hard negatives." arXiv preprint arXiv:1707.05612 (2017).\
>[3] Lee, Kuang-Huei, et al. "Stacked cross attention for image-text matching." Proceedings of the European conference on computer vision (ECCV). 2018.\

**Q8: it is unclear to me how to implement the proposed training objective.**

**R8:** For a clear presentation, we provide the python code of the proposed training objectives (i.e., $\mathcal{L}\_{uce}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{kl}$) as follows:
```python
class  UncertaintyAwareLoss(nn.Module):
    """
    Compute UncertaintyAwareLoss
    """
    def __init__(self, tau):
        super(UncertaintyAwareLoss, self).__init__()
        self.tau = tau

    def KL(self, alpha, K):
        beta = torch.ones((1, K)).cuda()
        S_alpha = torch.sum(alpha, dim=1, keepdim=True)
        S_beta = torch.sum(beta, dim=1, keepdim=True)
        lnB = torch.lgamma(S_alpha) - torch.sum(torch.lgamma(alpha), dim=1, keepdim=True)
        lnB_uni = torch.sum(torch.lgamma(beta), dim=1, keepdim=True) - torch.lgamma(S_beta)
        dg0 = torch.digamma(S_alpha)
        dg1 = torch.digamma(alpha)
        kl = torch.sum((alpha - beta) * (dg1 - dg0), dim=1, keepdim=True) + lnB + lnB_uni
        return kl

    # sims (K,K)
    def forward(self, sims, lambda_):
        K = sims.size(0)
        label = torch.eye(K)
        E = torch.exp(sims / self.tau)
        alpha = E + 1
        S = torch.sum(alpha, dim=1, keepdim=True)
        # L_uce loss
        A = torch.sum(label * (torch.digamma(S) - torch.digamma(alpha)), dim=1, keepdim=True)
        # L_kl loss
        alp = E * (1 - label) + 1
        B = lambda_ * self.KL(alp, K)
        return (A + B)

# For example
criterion = UncertaintyAwareLoss(0.05)
# img_embs1: visual embeddings of i2t branch; txs_embs1: textual embeddings of i2t branch
# img_embs2: visual embeddings of t2i branch; txs_embs2: textual embeddings of t2i branch
sims_i2t = sim_func(img_embs1, txs_embs1)      # compute visual-text similarity
sims_t2i = sim_func(img_embs2, txs_embs2).t()  # compute visual-text similarity
loss = UncertaintyAwareLoss.forward(sims_i2t,lambda_)
loss += UncertaintyAwareLoss.forward(sims_t2i,lambda_)
```

**Q6: It seems the whole paper is based on a cross-modal evidential learning framework. I would suggest the paper could first formally state the setting of this framework and emphasize the difference against the standard image text retrieval (contrastive learning) framework.**

**R6:** Thanks for your valuable suggestions. We have modified the corresponding content as per your suggestions in the revision (see Section 3.1). To be specific, the setting of our framework is to model the uncertainty for trustworthy image-text matching. To this end, TcVSE first utilizes evidential learning to quantify the uncertainty of VSE models, and then a consistency module to enforce bidirectional subjective opinions to provide better performance and uncertainty estimation. Therefore, our TcVSE could accurately measure not only the visual-textual similarity but also the retrieval uncertainty. However, the standard image text retrieval methods can only measure visual-textual similarity while being incapable of self-evaluation.

**Q7: harshly writing**

**R7:** Thank your detailed comments. We have revised the paper according to your suggestions. Our point-by-point response is listed as follows:

1. What is the image data augmentation mentioned in Sect. 2.1 page 3?\
   Ans: Following VSE$\infty$ [1], we conduct the same data augmentation strategy to manually amplify uncertainty in data, i.e., "Discard", "Mask", and "Swap". To be specific, for images, some extracted region proposals are randomly discarded according to a given probability. For sentences, some words are randomly discarded, masked, or swapped with each other. The data augmentation is only utilized during the training stage, but not during testing.

2. What is the meaning of 'However, almost these methods focus on unimodal classification'? Is it a typo for 'almost of'?\
   Ans: Yes, it is a typo. This sentence is 'However, these methods almost focus on unimodal classification and less touching image-text matching'. We have carefully checked and revised such typos in the paper.

3. Eq. 2 what is $s$?\
   Ans: $s$ is the image-text similarity, we have given the definition in the revision.

4. (a) What is the meaning of K-way querying? (b) What are the queries? (c) And why it is K-way?\
    Ans: (a) In a mini-batch with $K$ pairs,  "$K$-way querying" means the process of $K$ times independent searching/querying samples from another modality for a given query sample, wherein (b) the given query sample is viewed as a query. (c) Due to the huge number of image-text training pairs, we need to train the model and collect the evidence in a batch-by-batch manner when conducting evidential deep learning. 
  
5. (a) What is the evidence? (b) What is the function of the evidence?\
   Ans: In image-text matching, (a) the evidence could be considered as a measure of the amount of support collected from data in favor of retrieval/matching. Thus, the similarity can naturally be viewed as the source of evidence. (b) Then, the collected evidence will be used to parameterize the Dirichlet priors required for the subsequent evidential learning.

6. BiGUR -> BiGRU in implementation detail.\
   Sorry for the typo. We have carefully checked and revised the typos in the paper.
7. IMT -> ITM in the last paragraph of the introduction.\
   Thanks. We have revised the typo in the revision.

content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable comments and insightful suggestions. We have carefully looked into all the comments and suggestions. Attached is our point-by-point response.

**Q1: What is the definition of the uncertainty discussed through the whole paper?**

**R1:** In this paper, uncertainty refers to the degree of retrieval unreliability performed by the learned model, i.e., ``Is this retrieval trustworthy?'' stated in Section 1. The higher uncertainty means that the retrieved results are less reliable, and vice versa.

**Q2: What are the benefits of modeling the uncertainty? Why would we need to model the uncertainty on the image-text retrieval task?**

**R2:** The uncertainty could be utilized to evaluate the reliability of retrieved results, which could provide an additional self-evaluation metric except for similarity. That is to say, we could build a trusted cross-modal system benefitting from uncertainty estimation, which provides not only the retrieved results but also the reliability of this retrieval for self-evaluation. However, the existing image-text matching methods mainly focus on estimating accurate visual-textual similarity and then use it as the only criterion for retrieval. Thus, they cannot self-evaluate the quality of retrieved results for trustworthy retrieval, which is inappropriate in real-world scenarios due to the ubiquitous uncertainty, e.g., noise. In brief, we need to model the uncertainty of the image-text retrieval tasks for trustworthy retrieval.

**Q3: The benefits and the motivations of modeling uncertainty in the image-text domain.**

**R3:** In practice, the predictions of DNN models are not always reliable and may be overconfident in some wrong predictions, which limits their use in the industry. Thus, if we fully rely on deep models for decision-making, it will lead to disastrous consequences in some areas with high safety requirements, e.g., Auto Pilot System. Therefore, we need to self-evaluate the credibility of a prediction to make correct decisions, but this is less touched in the image-text community. To address the problem, we present an uncertainty-aware method to estimate the credibility of predictions, which could assign a higher uncertainty for wrong/unreliable predictions even with high prediction values, and vice versa.

**Q4: Why the approach achieves faster processing speed than VSE$\infty$?**

**R4:** GPO of VSE$\infty$ is more time-consuming than other aggregation strategies, which has been discussed in [1]. Specifically, parametric GPO requires extra computation cost to calculate the weight coefficients before aggregating features, while non-parametric pooling methods (e.g., $Max Pooling$ and $Avg Pooling$) could directly perform aggregations. To quantize the difference, we replace $Max Pooling$ with GPO in TcVSE for inference. The comparison results in terms of time cost are shown in the following table, wherein one could find that the computational cost of GPO is indeed higher than that of $Max Pooling$.

| Method   | Configuration| Cost time |
|---|----|--|
| VSE$\infty$ |   | 3s  |
| TcVSE | one branch  | 2s    |
|| two branches | 4s |
| TcVSE with GPO | one branch  | 3s |
|| two branches | 4.3s  |


**Q5: This paper seems not mention the difference of the architecture between the proposed approach and the state-of-the-art model (e.g. VSE$\infty$). I wonder whether the performance improvement is due to the architecture difference or the proposed uncertainty estimation loss?**

**R5:** Thanks for your valuable suggestion. The difference has been supplemented in the Implementation Detail (Section 3.1). The basic framework of our TcVSE is similar to that of VSE$\infty$, but the difference is the aggregation strategy and the uncertainty-aware loss $\mathcal{L}_{u}$. First, we found that using GPO in our method did not achieve better results than using $MaxPooling$. Thus, we chose $MaxPooling$ with less cost as our aggregation strategy. The specific comparison is shown as follows:

|---|----|----|----|----|--|---|---|
|  | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | R@1   | R@5   | R@10  | rSum   |
| TcVSE   | 80.3  | 95.5  | 97.8  | 59.7  | 85.1  | 90.9  | 509.3  |
| TcVSE with GPO | 80.7  | 95.1  | 97.9  | 59.3  | 84.9  | 91.1  | 509.0  |

| VSE$\infty$          | 76.5  | 94.2  | 97.7  | 56.4  | 83.4  | 89.9  | 498.1  |


Second, our uncertainty-aware loss also could boost the retrieval performance by capturing the uncertainty in data. To verify the effectiveness, we provide the experimental results without the proposed loss in the above table. From the results, one could find that the performance will be remarkably degraded, which indicates that our loss could provide a performance improvement. 

In conclusion, performance improvement is only brought by the proposed loss, while efficiency improvement is brought by architectural differences.

Thanks for your valuable comments and insightful suggestions. Attached is our point-by-point response.

**Q1: In addition to VSE framework, can other image-text models use the uncertainty estimation module? For example CLIP model.**

**R1:** Yes. In past years, Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) has proven its effectiveness by qualifying uncertainty in many tasks, e.g. classification [3] and action recognization [4]. In this paper, we have demonstrated its effectiveness for cross-modal retrieval by capturing the uncertainty. Moreover, the proposed uncertainty loss is a generalized objective function, which could be easily plugged into other image-text models for uncertainty estimation. To demonstrate the feasibility, we have extended a fine-grained image-text matching method SGRAF (SAF and SGR) [5] by our uncertainty estimation module. The results are shown as follows. Due to time and computation limitations, we are not able to train the big model on large-scale data.

**R2:** Thanks to the big models and large-scale training data, the pre-trained models have achieved excellent performance, such as UNICODER [1]. However, the large cost of training and even fine-tuning is prohibitive, especially for video memory (VRAM). For example, it costs about 4GB VRAM to train our model with Bi-GRU, which could be easily satisfied in most consumer GPUs. However, UNICODER requires 4 V100 GPUs with 32GB VRAM to train, which is not applicable to ordinary users. Unavoidably, due to a much smaller model and much less training data, the performance of lightweight models have commonly inferior performance to that of pre-trained models. In this paper, we mainly focus on lightweight models in image-text matching, which is more friendly for ordinary users and some resource-restricted applications. Although our method is inferior to the big pre-trained models, it is superior to all the lightweight image-text methods, especially improving the performance of VSE-based methods to a new level. In the revision, we have supplemented the related works about big pre-trained image-text models. As the feasibility mentioned above R2, we think that our framework could be used in the training or fine-tuning of UNICODER to endow it with the uncertainty-aware ability for cross-modal retrieval. content.comment:
**Q3: The qualitative results are somewhat concerning to me, and I think the two datasets are not best suited to evaluate this task. See Figure 4.c. The top 1 and even all top 4 sentences look correct/plausible to me (GT says only 1 is correct). Therefore I’m not sure how this kind of ambiguous annotation could have impacted the model. Also, would removing data augmentation during training change the behavior of the model (I understand Figure 3 shows this on the test set)? Please elaborate on this.**

**R3:** Thanks. In real-world scenarios, such ambiguous retrieval results may induce unsatisfactory even incorrect decisions, which is the motivation of this paper. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework to estimate the uncertainty/ambiguity of the retrieval results, thus providing a risk assessment for unsatisfactory decisions. In Figure 4(c), although some retrieved results (see below) seem to be acceptable, they are partial and ambiguous. To be specific, there are three people (two men and one woman) in the image, but they only infer two men while ignoring the one woman in the corner. Thus, they cannot retrieve more appropriate results (i.e., GTs) in the retrieval database, e.g., "Three people at with their backs to the camera at an internet bar .", "Three people are sitting at a counter using laptop computers ."，“Three people work on their laptops inside a store .”, etc. As shown below, our method could infer a relatively high uncertainty score (0.8273) for these ambiguous results, which could remind users that the retrieval (decision) is less confident (unreliable). Therefore, people could decide whether human intervention is needed for correct decisions based on the inferred uncertainty scores, but less touched in most deterministic deep models.

1. Two men looking at a computer . (False, 0.2822)
2. There are two men and one female sitting down and looking at their laptops in front of a window .(True, 0.2548)
3. Two men are discussing something . (False, 0.2501)
4. Two men sitting and talking to each other .(False, 0.2389) 
5. Two men are in a room and are looking in
opposite directions . (False, 0.1790)

Yes, removing data augmentation will change the behavior of the model as shown in follows. In the training stage, data augmentation is utilized to artificially amplify the perturbation/uncertainty in the training data to strengthen the ability of the modal to capture uncertainty. Therefore, removing data augmentation will degrade the performance of uncertainty estimation. To clarify the influence, we retrain the model without data augmentation, and perform sentence retrieval of the image in Figure 4(c). The retrieved results are listed as follows. From the new results, one could find that the model without data augmentation infers higher similarities and lower uncertainty for incorrect retrieval, which is bad for ambiguous cases. Therefore, the manually injected uncertainty in training data could help the model capture the uncertainty, thus embracing a reasonable measurement of uncertainty.

The overall uncertainty is 0.6802, and retrievals are
1. Two men looking at a computer . (False, 0.4293)
2. Two men are discussing something . (False, 0.4081)
3. Two men sitting and talking to each other . (False, 0.3915)
4. Two men are watching something . (False, 0.3600)
5. There are two men and one female sitting down and looking at their laptops in front of a window . (True, 0.2950)

Furthermore, the purpose of data augmentation in Figure 3 is different from that in training. Since the intrinsic uncertainty/perturbation in data is uncontrollable and inconspicuous, it is hard to quantitatively evaluate the uncertainty. Thus, we artificially inject perturbation of given ratios into test data to quantitatively investigate the ability of our method to capture the uncertainty in different ratios of unreliable data as shown in Figure 3. The results demonstrate our method could well quantify the uncertainty in data.
